name: Experimenter Bias
description: A researcher's expectations can unintentionally shape what participants do or how outcomes are observed, recorded, or interpreted. The study starts leaning toward the hoped-for answer before the analysis even begins.
design_relevance_note: Highly relevant to moderated usability testing, interview protocols, diary studies, synthetic evaluations, and experiment readouts where researcher cues or leading expectations can distort the evidence teams think they collected.
myth_risk_note: Barber et al.'s five-attempt replication study found the experimenter-bias effect difficult to reproduce consistently, suggesting the phenomenon, while real in its original demonstration, is less robust across contexts and replication attempts than its wide citation implies.
prevalence_note: A standard warning in UX research and experimentation practice, especially around moderation bias, observer effects, and the need for blinding or structured protocols.

findings.description: Student experimenters who believed their rats were 'maze-bright' versus 'maze-dull' obtained performance differences consistent with those expectations even though the animals had been randomly assigned, demonstrating that experimenter expectations can shape measured outcomes.
findings.source_title: The effect of experimenter bias on the performance of the albino rat

findings.description: Using text mining and literature review across the life sciences, Holman, Head, Lanfear & Jennions independently confirm the core experimenter-expectancy mechanism Rosenthal & Fode demonstrated in a single rat-maze study: non-blind studies (where researchers know subjects' treatment/identity) report systematically higher effect sizes and more statistically significant results than blind studies, at a much larger meta-scientific scale, and find blind data-recording protocols remain uncommon across the life sciences.
findings.source_title: Evidence of Experimental Bias in the Life Sciences: Why We Need Blind Data Recording

applications.title: Clever Hans: the 'arithmetic horse' whose owner unconsciously cued every answer
applications.description: Clever Hans was a horse in early-20th-century Germany whose owner, Wilhelm von Osten, claimed could perform arithmetic, identify colors, and read. Psychologist Oscar Pfungst investigated the case in 1907 and found that Hans only answered correctly when his questioner already knew the correct answer -- Hans was responding to subtle, unconscious cues from the questioner, not actually performing the claimed cognitive feats. The case became the namesake for the 'Clever Hans effect,' a foundational example of the observer-expectancy effect (experimenter bias).
applications.ethical_note: This documents the foundational historical case for observer-expectancy/experimenter bias, not a persuasion or product-design scenario -- included because it is the namesake case for this exact bias and remains the clearest illustration of how unconscious expectations can contaminate results without any deliberate intent to deceive.
